title: Malachi 1:1–5
context: Malachi’s message unfolds in disputations: the LORD makes a statement, the people answer, “Yet you say …,” and the LORD replies. The first sets the tone. The LORD says, “I have loved you”; the people ask, “How have you loved us?”; and the LORD answers by pointing to Jacob and Esau and to Edom’s ruined land (1:2–4), so that Israel will confess, “The LORD is great—even beyond the border of Israel!” (1:5). Paul cites 1:2–3 in Romans 9:13; see the existing Romans 9:13 box. Edom’s desolation and its later history are held with care.

verses.text: A revelation, the LORD’s word to Israel by Malachi.
verses.arminianNotes: The heading calls the book “A revelation, the LORD’s word to Israel by Malachi.” Arminian readers see a message addressed to a real community after the exile, calling them back to wholehearted faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD speaking to Israel through his messenger. Shared ground: the book presents itself as the LORD’s word, and its rebukes and promises carry his authority.

verses.text: “I have loved you,” says the LORD. Yet you say, “How have you loved us?” “Wasn’t Esau Jacob’s brother?” says the LORD, “Yet I loved Jacob;
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “I have loved you,” and the people answer, “How have you loved us?” Arminian readers hear covenant love toward Israel as a people, set against Edom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise begin with God’s love declared and questioned. Paul cites this verse in Romans 9:13. Shared ground: Israel’s standing rests on the LORD’s prior love.

verses.text: but Esau I hated, and made his mountains a desolation, and gave his heritage to the jackals of the wilderness.”
verses.arminianNotes: “but Esau I hated, and made his mountains a desolation,” Arminian readers commonly take “hated” as a strong idiom for not choosing Esau’s line, applied here to Edom as a nation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise take “hated” as strong idiom rather than personal malice, and read the verse with Paul in Romans 9:13. Edom’s desolation was evident in Malachi’s day, though its exact historical course is held with care.

verses.text: Whereas Edom says, “We are beaten down, but we will return and build the waste places,” the LORD of Armies says, “They shall build, but I will throw down; and men will call them ‘The Wicked Land,’ even the people against whom the LORD shows wrath forever.”
verses.arminianNotes: Edom says, “We are beaten down, but we will return and build the waste places,” yet the LORD answers, “They shall build, but I will throw down.” Arminian readers see human resolve unable to overturn God’s judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s word prevailing over Edom’s plans. Readers in this tradition note the long hostility between Edom and Israel recalled in Obadiah 10, cited by reference, while holding details of Edom’s history with care.

verses.text: Your eyes will see, and you will say, “The LORD is great—even beyond the border of Israel!”
verses.arminianNotes: “Your eyes will see, and you will say, ‘The LORD is great—even beyond the border of Israel!’” Arminian readers see Israel brought to recognize God’s love through his dealings with the nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s greatness displayed beyond Israel’s borders. Shared ground: the answer to the people’s doubt is a renewed vision of the LORD’s greatness and faithfulness.
